# Repository Analysis: bikini/exploitarium

## Purpose
This is a consolidated archive of public proof-of-concept exploits and vulnerability research compiled by a security researcher. The maintainer states it was created to attract newcomers to cybersecurity research.

## Scope
The repository contains approximately 50+ different vulnerability PoCs affecting diverse software, including:

- **Browsers**: Firefox, Ladybird
- **Utilities**: ffmpeg, ImageMagick, VLC, nmap, objdump
- **Infrastructure**: Docker, QEMU, OpenSSH, OpenVPN
- **Web platforms**: Discourse, Gogs, Gitea, NextCloud, NextJS
- **Communication**: Discord, RustDesk, AnyDesk
- **Databases**: Redis, PostgreSQL
- **Libraries**: libssh2, c-ares, libarchive, curl, nghttp2

## CVE Status
The maintainer explicitly states: "At the time I post these, none have been reported." The repository includes a `cves.md` file, though specific CVE/GHSA identifiers are not listed in the provided content.

## Important Disclaimer
The author emphasizes: "Do NOT, under any circumstances, use any material in this repository maliciously." All material is characterized as good-faith, coordinated disclosure research intended for educational purposes.

The repository contains 66 commits and has 4.1k stars as of the page snapshot.

# DataQ backend — runtime dependencies (SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH).
#
# Everything else points here: `environment.yml` (via requirements-dev.txt), the
# CI test + audit jobs, and the production Docker image. Bump a runtime version
# HERE only.
#
# Two pip files reference these versions and stay aligned automatically:

#                                   the typecheck-deps-sync CI check guards the
#                                   pre-commit mypy hook against this subset.

# ── Web framework ──
fastapi==0.139.2
uvicorn[standard]==0.51.0
python-multipart==0.0.32          # required for FastAPI form data; CVE-2026-24486/40347/42561 (was 0.0.20)

# ── Task queue ──
celery[redis]==5.6.3
redis==5.3.1
croniter==6.2.4                   # cron-expression parsing for suite run schedules (A7)

# ── Database ──
sqlalchemy==2.0.51
alembic==1.18.5
psycopg2-binary==2.9.12           # swap for psycopg2 in the production image

# ── Config / validation ──
pydantic==2.13.4
pydantic-settings==2.14.2

# ── DQ engine (PINNED — GX v1 API drifts across point releases) ──
great-expectations==1.17.2

# ── Observability ──
structlog==26.1.0
opentelemetry-sdk==1.43.0                        # spans (A3) + logs (#524) — vendor-neutral core, ADR 0010
opentelemetry-instrumentation-fastapi==0.64b0    # server span per request
opentelemetry-instrumentation-celery==0.64b0     # span per task run
azure-monitor-opentelemetry-exporter==1.0.0b55   # Azure backend for spans + logs (exporter ONLY, not the distro — it would double-configure the log pipeline)
opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http==1.43.0   # generic OTLP/HTTP backend for spans + logs (#589) — any OTLP consumer (Tempo/Jaeger/Datadog), vendor-neutral (ADR 0010)

# ── Auth / secrets ──
fastapi-azure-auth==5.2.0
msal==1.37.0                      # ≥1.34 lifts the cryptography<47 cap → unblocks cryptography≥48 (#274)
azure-keyvault-secrets==4.11.0
azure-identity==1.25.3

# ── Datasource connectors ──
snowflake-sqlalchemy==1.11.0       # ≥1.8 lifts the connector<4.0 cap (#129)
snowflake-connector-python==4.7.1  # 3→4: drops cffi<2 / pyOpenSSL<26 caps → unblocks cryptography≥46.0.7 + pyOpenSSL≥26 CVE fixes (#129)
cryptography==49.0.0               # direct floor — transitive (snowflake/pyOpenSSL/azure/GX); pins past GHSA-537c-gmf6-5ccf in 46.0.7 (#274)
azure-storage-blob==12.30.0       # ADLS Gen2
boto3==1.43.46                    # S3
databricks-sql-connector==4.3.0   # Unity Catalog
databricks-sqlalchemy==2.0.10      # the SQLAlchemy 'databricks' dialect — SPLIT OUT of the connector in 4.x (#535); bump the pair together
pyarrow==24.0.0                   # Parquet flat-file IO (read_parquet/profiler) — was a databricks-sql-connector transitive until its 4.x dropped it (#201)
pyiceberg[pyarrow]==0.11.1        # native Iceberg read (ADR 0030, #716) — v2 baseline; spike-verified compatible with pyarrow 24 + GX 1.17.2 (#286); its rich<15/cachetools<7 transitives were unpinned, CVE-clean per pip-audit
openpyxl==3.1.5                   # XLSX comparison-report download (ADR 0015 §4, #795) — derived on demand, never stored. MIT (rule 40); lazy-imported on the download path only
adlfs==2026.5.0                   # pyiceberg FileIO for abfss:// (ADLS) warehouses — [pyarrow] covers S3 natively but resolves ADLS via fsspec/adlfs; without it any ADLS-warehouse iceberg table load dies ModuleNotFoundError (#749). BSD-3 (rule 40)

# ── Lineage (OpenLineage emission — ADR 0034 / #758) ──
openlineage-python==1.51.0        # Apache-2.0 (rule 40); emits DQ RunEvents, dark by default. Core deps only (attrs/requests/httpx/pyyaml/python-dateutil/packaging) — no kafka/gcp extras

fastmcp==3.4.4                    # CVE-2025-62800/62801/64340/69196, GHSA-rcfx-77hg-w2wv, CVE-2026-27124 (was 2.8.1)

This entry documents command execution through Redis Vector Set RDB loading when serialized HNSW nodes reuse the same node ID. The PoC starts an unmodified Redis binary, drives the exploit path over Redis TCP commands, and writes a marker file from code executed inside the Redis process.

## Target

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Product | Redis |
| Tested commit | `5b22a09918743ba72952e35e431db23eb3d19605` |
| Tested binary | `Redis server v=255.255.255 sha=5b22a099:0 malloc=libc bits=64 build=c8d40b9af9f5dac8` |
| Platform | Linux x86-64 |
| Allocator | libc malloc |
| Redis configuration used by the PoC | `enable-debug-command no`, `sanitize-dump-payload yes`, no persistence |
| Command surface | `RESTORE`, `VREM`, `VLINKS`, `SET`, `SETRANGE`, `DEL`, `EVAL` |

The local launcher uses the child process map and local ELF metadata to resolve the Redis PIE base, `free@GOT`, libc, and `system`. The heap corruption, read oracle, overwrite, and command execution trigger are all performed through Redis protocol commands sent to the selected stock `redis-server` process.

## Root Cause

Vector Set module deserialization accepts multiple serialized HNSW nodes that share the same node ID. During index deserialization, the ID lookup table stores only one node for each ID, while the element dictionary stores nodes by element name. Link validation then reasons about node IDs rather than enforcing a one-to-one relationship between ID and node object.

After the key is restored, removing the dictionary-visible node for a duplicated ID leaves other HNSW links pointing at the freed allocation. Those stale links remain reachable through graph operations. A quantized Vector Set turns one stale link into a stable 64-bit read oracle through `VLINKS ... WITHSCORES`. A second Vector Set uses two stale neighbors during `hnsw_reconnect_nodes()` to write attacker-selected pointers into a live module value. Deleting the corrupted key reaches `freeModuleObject()`, which dispatches through the overwritten module type pointer.

## Source Trace

| File | Relevant path |
| --- | --- |
| `modules/vector-sets/vset.c` | `hnsw_insert_serialized()` inserts restored nodes into the element dictionary before `hnsw_deserialize_index()` resolves HNSW links. |
| `modules/vector-sets/hnsw.c` | `hnsw_deserialize_index()` populates the node-ID table and validates links by ID, allowing duplicate IDs to alias distinct node objects. |
| `modules/vector-sets/hnsw.c` | `hnsw_delete_node()` calls `hnsw_reconnect_nodes()` while stale duplicate-ID neighbors are still reachable from the removed node's link array. |
| `modules/vector-sets/vset.c` | `VLINKS_RedisCommand()` exposes neighbor distances, which the PoC uses as the bit-by-bit read oracle. |
| `src/object.c` | `freeModuleObject()` calls `mv->type->free(mv->value)`, which becomes the final control-flow target after the module value overwrite. |

## Exploit Flow

1. Start the requested `redis-server` binary with a temporary configuration.
2. Use a malformed Vector Set `RESTORE` payload with duplicate HNSW IDs.
3. Remove one duplicate element with `VREM`, leaving a stale HNSW link.
4. Reclaim the freed node with a Redis string that is shaped as a fake HNSW node.
5. Use `VLINKS ... WITHSCORES` against 65 mask nodes to recover a 64-bit value from an attacker-selected address.
6. Leak `free@GOT`, derive libc, and resolve `system`.
7. Walk Redis keyspace structures with the read oracle to locate the Vector Set module value and two controlled string allocations.
8. Restore a second malformed Vector Set with two stale neighbors.
9. Reclaim both freed nodes with Redis strings shaped as fake HNSW nodes.
10. Trigger `hnsw_reconnect_nodes()` with `VREM` so the fake nodes overwrite `moduleValue->type` and `moduleValue->value`.
11. Delete the corrupted key so `freeModuleObject()` invokes `system()` with the controlled command buffer.

## Usage

Build Redis on Linux with libc malloc, then run:

```bash
python3 poc.py \
  --redis-server /path/to/redis/src/redis-server \
  --work-dir /tmp/redis-vset-rce \
  --port 6631
```

The PoC writes the marker file `R` inside the selected work directory. The marker is created by the command executed from inside the Redis process:

```text
uid=1000(owner) gid=1000(owner) groups=1000(owner),4(adm),24(cdrom),27(sudo),30(dip),46(plugdev),100(users)
```

## Local Verification

The committed PoC was replayed from this folder against a fresh stock build:

```text
/mnt/d/exploitarium/redis-vset-duplicate-hnsw-id-rce-poc/poc.py
/mnt/d/redis-rce-validation/redis-wsl/src/redis-server
Redis server v=255.255.255 sha=5b22a099:0 malloc=libc bits=64 build=c8d40b9af9f5dac8
```

Representative output is saved in [`evidence/local-verification.txt`](evidence/local-verification.txt).

## Files

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| [`poc.py`](poc.py) | Self-contained Redis Vector Set RCE proof. |
| [`evidence/local-verification.txt`](evidence/local-verification.txt) | Output from a successful local stock Redis replay. |

## Notes

The script is intentionally local-process oriented: it launches Redis, observes that launched process, and tears it down after the run. For long work paths, it uses a short temporary runtime directory and links `R` back to the requested work directory so the payload command can remain `id > R`. The payload produces a benign proof marker in the work directory.

Only run this against systems you own or have explicit permission to test.

[Resource from github at repo://bikini/exploitarium/sha/cdcbe772ed7ee2a36f2d84a93018f820a32a4a9f/contents/postgres-ri-owner-switched-cast-poc/README.md] # PostgreSQL RI Owner-Switched Implicit Cast PoC

This entry documents server-side command execution through PostgreSQL referential-integrity checking when a foreign-key column uses an attacker-owned implicit cast into the referenced primary-key operator class type.

The PoC drives a normal PostgreSQL server through `psql`. It creates the owner and attacker roles, grants column-level `REFERENCES` on the primary-key column, creates the attacker-owned type, SQL function, implicit cast, and foreign-key table, then inserts a row that forces the RI lookup to invoke the cast function while the effective database role is the referenced table owner.

## Target

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Product | PostgreSQL |
| Tested commit | `e0ff7fd9aa2e6f77c38825e71200ced742220d55` |
| Tested binary | `PostgreSQL 20devel on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu` |
| Platform | Linux x86-64 |
| Interface | `psql` against a stock server |
| Required owner capability for the payload | membership in `pg_execute_server_program` |
| Required attacker grant on the referenced table | `REFERENCES (id)` |

## Impact

An attacker who can create a data type, SQL function, implicit cast, and referencing table can place attacker-owned SQL in the FK type-to-PK type cast path. When a row is inserted into the referencing table, PostgreSQL's RI check switches to the referenced table owner before it probes the referenced table. The implicit cast is then invoked as a normal `SECURITY INVOKER` SQL function under that owner-switched effective role.

If the referenced table owner has `pg_execute_server_program`, the attacker-owned SQL function can reach `COPY ... TO PROGRAM`. The PoC writes a marker containing `current_user`, `session_user`, and `is_superuser`; a successful run produces:

```text
ri_owner_probe:ri_attacker_probe:off
```

## Source Trace

| File | Relevant path |
| --- | --- |
| `src/backend/commands/functioncmds.c` | `CreateCast()` allows cast creation when the caller owns the source or target type and records `AS IMPLICIT` casts in `pg_cast`. |
| `src/backend/commands/tablecmds.c` | FK creation accepts an implicit cast from the FK type to the primary-key operator-class input type through `can_coerce_type(..., COERCION_IMPLICIT)`. |
| `src/backend/commands/tablecmds.c` | Referenced-table permission checks accept table-level or column-level `REFERENCES`. |
| `src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c` | `ri_PlanCheck()` and `ri_PerformCheck()` switch to the owner of the table being queried for RI enforcement. |
| `src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c` | `ri_FastPathCheck()` and `ri_FastPathBatchFlush()` switch to the referenced table owner before building scan keys and probing the PK index. |
| `src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c` | `build_index_scankeys()` calls the cached cast function for FK values that must be coerced to the operator input type. |
| `src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c` | `ri_CompareWithCast()` and `ri_HashCompareOp()` resolve and call implicit cast functions during RI comparisons. |
| `src/backend/executor/functions.c` | SQL functions reject client-side `COPY`, while file and program `COPY` utility statements continue into normal execution. |
| `src/backend/executor/spi.c` | SPI rejects client-side `COPY` and permits filename/program `COPY` utility statements to proceed. |
| `src/backend/commands/copy.c` | `COPY TO/FROM PROGRAM` checks `pg_execute_server_program` against `GetUserId()`. |
| `src/backend/commands/copyto.c` | A permitted `COPY TO PROGRAM` reaches `OpenPipeStream()`. |

The relevant owner switch in `ri_PerformCheck()` sets the active user ID to the owner of the relation being queried. The foreign-key insert path queries the referenced table, so the active user ID becomes the referenced table owner before the implicit cast executes.

## Reproduction Flow

1. Connect as a bootstrap database role that can create roles, create a database, and grant `pg_execute_server_program`.
2. Create `ri_owner_probe` and grant it `pg_execute_server_program`.
3. Create `ri_attacker_probe`.
4. Create `ri_owner_probe.pk(id integer primary key)` and insert `7`.
5. Grant `REFERENCES (id)` on `ri_owner_probe.pk` to `ri_attacker_probe`.
6. As `ri_attacker_probe`, create a composite type, a SQL cast function, an implicit cast from that type to `integer`, and a referencing table.
7. Confirm a direct call to the cast function is blocked by the `COPY TO PROGRAM` privilege check.
8. Insert `ROW(7)::ri_attacker_probe.fkkey` into the FK table.
9. Confirm that the marker file was created with `current_user` equal to the referenced table owner and `session_user` equal to the attacker role.

## Usage

Start a stock PostgreSQL server and run the PoC with a bootstrap role:

```bash
python3 poc.py \
  --psql /path/to/psql \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 5432 \
  --admin-user postgres \
  --admin-db postgres \
  --marker /tmp/postgres_ri_cast_marker.txt
```

If the bootstrap role requires a password, pass it through the environment:

```bash
PGPASSWORD='REDACTED' python3 poc.py --admin-user postgres
```

The marker path is interpreted by the PostgreSQL server host because it is used inside `COPY ... TO PROGRAM`.

Expected output shape:

```json
{
  "database": "ri_cast_probe",
  "owner_role": "ri_owner_probe",
  "attacker_role": "ri_attacker_probe",
  "direct_function_call_blocked": true,
  "insert_returncode": 0,
  "marker": "ri_owner_probe:ri_attacker_probe:off",
  "expected_marker": "ri_owner_probe:ri_attacker_probe:off",
  "reproduced": true
}
```

## Local Verification

The committed PoC was replayed from this folder against a fresh stock PostgreSQL build:

```text
PostgreSQL 20devel on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu
commit e0ff7fd9aa2e6f77c38825e71200ced742220d55
```

Representative output is saved in [`evidence/local-verification.txt`](evidence/local-verification.txt).

## Files

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| [`poc.py`](poc.py) | End-to-end PostgreSQL RI implicit-cast proof. |
| [`evidence/local-verification.txt`](evidence/local-verification.txt) | Output from a successful local replay against a stock PostgreSQL server. |

## Notes

The script drops and recreates the probe database and two probe roles named in the command-line options. Run it against a disposable database instance or use role/database names reserved for this validation.

Only run this against systems you own or have explicit permission to test.

    def publish_health(self, session: Session, report: ConnectionHealthReport) -> None:
        """Email a connection poll-health edge to the **workspace** recipients (#837).

        A connection has no suite, so there is no per-suite recipient override to
        resolve — this goes to ``EMAIL_TO``. Quiet no-op when the SMTP transport or the
        workspace recipient list is unconfigured.
        """
        if not (self._username and self._password_secret_name and self._sender):
            return
        if not self._recipients:
            return
        try:
            password = self._secret_store.get(self._password_secret_name)
        except SecretNotFoundError:
            log.warning("email_password_unresolved", secret_name=self._password_secret_name)
            return
        message = self._message(
            subject=render_health_subject(report),
            recipients=self._recipients,
            text=render_health_text_body(report),
            html=render_health_html_body(report),
        )
        self._send(message, password=password)
        log.info(
            "email_health_alert_sent",
            connection_id=str(report.connection_id),
            state=report.state,
            recipients=len(self._recipients),
        )

    def _message(
        self, *, subject: str, recipients: tuple[str, ...], text: str, html: str
    ) -> EmailMessage:
        """A multipart text+HTML message from this publisher's sender to ``recipients``."""
        message = EmailMessage()
        message["Subject"] = subject
        message["From"] = self._sender
        message["To"] = ", ".join(recipients)
        message.set_content(text)
        message.add_alternative(html, subtype="html")
        return message

    def _send(self, message: EmailMessage, *, password: str) -> None:
        """SMTP submission over STARTTLS. Shared by the run + health paths so the
        transport (and its TLS context) is implemented exactly once — a security
        property that must not be able to differ between two copies of it."""
        context = ssl.create_default_context()
        with smtplib.SMTP(self._smtp_host, self._smtp_port, timeout=self._timeout) as server:
            server.starttls(context=context)
            # mypy: guarded by the transport check in both callers.
            server.login(self._username or "", password)
            server.send_message(message)

[Resource from github at repo://bikini/exploitarium/sha/cdcbe772ed7ee2a36f2d84a93018f820a32a4a9f/contents/flowise-mcp-env-case-bypass-poc/README.md] # Flowise 3.1.2 Custom MCP Environment Variable Case Bypass PoC

This repository documents and validates an authenticated Windows ACE/RCE-class issue in Flowise `3.1.2` / `flowise-components` `3.1.2`.

Flowise Custom MCP stdio validation blocks dangerous environment variable names such as `NODE_OPTIONS` by exact string comparison. Windows treats environment variable names case-insensitively. A casing variant such as `node_options` passes Flowise validation and is still honored by a spawned Node.js child process as `NODE_OPTIONS`.

## Affected Target

- Product: Flowise
- Version analyzed: `3.1.2`
- Package: `flowise-components@3.1.2`
- Platform impact: Windows Flowise deployments
- Required access: authenticated Flowise session or API-key context that can configure or load a Custom MCP stdio node

## Impact

An authenticated user who can reach Custom MCP stdio configuration can bypass the intended environment denylist and influence Node.js child process startup. When the MCP command is a Node.js process, a lower-case `node_options` entry can preload attacker-chosen JavaScript through Node's startup option handling.

The result is code execution in the Flowise worker/server context on Windows deployments where the Custom MCP path is reachable.

## Source Trace

Relevant source locations in Flowise `3.1.2`:

| File | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/components/nodes/tools/MCP/CustomMCP/CustomMCP.ts` | Parses `mcpServerConfig`, validates it when `CUSTOM_MCP_SECURITY_CHECK` is enabled, and creates `MCPToolkit` with stdio when a command is present |
| `packages/components/nodes/tools/MCP/core.ts` | `MCPToolkit.createClient` passes `serverParams.env` into `StdioClientTransport` |
| `packages/components/nodes/tools/MCP/core.ts` | `validateEnvironmentVariables` denies `PATH`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH`, and `NODE_OPTIONS` by exact-case comparison |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/stdio.js` | The stdio transport spawns the configured process with the supplied environment |

The vulnerable validation shape is:

```ts
const dangerousEnvVars = ['PATH', 'LD_LIBRARY_PATH', 'DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH', 'NODE_OPTIONS']

for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(env)) {
    if (dangerousEnvVars.includes(key)) {
        throw new Error(...)
    }
}
```

On Windows, `node_options` and `NODE_OPTIONS` address the same environment variable slot for the child process, but only the exact uppercase spelling is denied.

## PoC Design

`poc.py` models the relevant Flowise validation and then launches a local Node.js process with `node_options=--require <loader>`. The loader writes a marker file. On Windows, marker creation proves that the lower-case environment variable bypasses exact-case validation and is honored by Node.js as a startup option.

The script also shows the fix shape by comparing the vulnerable exact-case validator to a normalized validator that checks `key.upper()`.

## Requirements

- Python 3.10 or newer
- Node.js available in `PATH` for the canary execution step
- Windows for full child-process behavior reproduction

## Usage

Run the PoC:

```powershell
python poc.py
```

Run with a custom marker path:

```powershell
python poc.py --marker C:\Temp\flowise_marker.txt
```

Expected Windows output shape:

```json
{
  "windows": true,
  "flowise_style_exact_upper_blocked": true,
  "flowise_style_lower_variant_accepted": true,
  "normalized_validator_blocks_lower_variant": true,
  "node_canary": {
    "canary_created": true,
    "canary_content": "node_options honored"
  },
  "finding_reproduced": true
}
```

## Exploit Preconditions

- The deployment runs on Windows.
- Custom MCP stdio support is reachable.
- The attacker has an authenticated/session/API-key path that can influence a Custom MCP node configuration.
- The configured MCP command starts a Node.js child process or another runtime with security-sensitive environment handling.

## Root Cause

The denylist comparison is platform-insensitive. Environment variable names are case-sensitive on many Unix-like systems but case-insensitive on Windows. A security check that compares environment keys by exact string spelling does not enforce the intended policy on Windows.

## Fix Direction

- Normalize environment variable names before comparison on every platform.
- Use platform-aware comparison rules when validating environment keys.
- Prefer an allowlist of safe environment variables for MCP stdio child processes.
- Add Windows-specific regression tests for case variants such as `node_options`, `Node_Options`, and `NoDe_OpTiOnS`.

## Validation Status

The issue was locally validated against `flowise-components@3.1.2`: exact uppercase `NODE_OPTIONS` was blocked, lowercase `node_options` was accepted, and the MCP stdio path created a marker file through Node.js startup option handling.

content.text:
## Verdict: not impacted

`bikini/exploitarium` is a dump of ~44 self-published PoCs (4.1k stars, 12 assigned CVEs in `cves.md`, the rest claimed as unreported). I enumerated the actual directory listing via the GitHub API rather than trusting the page summary, then checked each entry against DataQ's real dependency graph. Nothing lands.

**The four entries that touch our stack, and why each misses:**

| PoC | Our reality | Why not exploitable |
|---|---|---|
| `redis-vset-duplicate-hnsw-id-rce` | `redis:7-alpine` (compose + [redis.tf:43](deploy/terraform/azure/redis.tf#L43)) | Bug is in the **Vector Sets module**, bundled from Redis **8**. Redis 7 has no `VSET`/`VLINKS` surface at all. Also needs an authenticated client: our broker is `external_enabled = false` + `--requirepass`. |
| `postgres-ri-owner-switched-cast` | PG 16 local / Azure Flexible Server prod | Needs a **hostile DB role** that can `CREATE TYPE/FUNCTION/CAST` and holds `REFERENCES`, *plus* a referenced-table owner in `pg_execute_server_program`. We have one least-priv `dataq_app` role and no untrusted roles; Azure doesn't grant `pg_execute_server_program`. Tested against 20devel. |
| `curl-smtp-expn-recipient-crlf-injection` | [email.py:316](backend/app/alerting/email.py#L316) uses Python `smtplib`, not libcurl | Not the same code path — and the analogous risk in *our* code is already closed: user-supplied recipients are CRLF-rejected at write time by `_UNSAFE_IN_RECIPIENT` ([notification_service.py:120](backend/app/services/notification_service.py#L120), from the #639 review). |
| `flowise-mcp-env-case-bypass` | Our MCP is a FastMCP **server** at `/mcp` | Flowise spawns stdio children from user config with an env denylist; we never spawn a child process from user input and have no env denylist. |

That last one is a class worth checking rather than a package match — a case-**sensitive** list matched against a case-**insensitive** value. I audited our three such lists and all normalize both sides: webhook SSRF hosts lowercase config ([:58](backend/app/services/notification_service.py#L58)) *and* parsed host ([:83](backend/app/services/notification_service.py#L83)), and the workspace-admin allowlist matches case-insensitively ([auth.py:283](backend/app/core/auth.py#L283)). They're allowlists too, so the failure mode is fail-closed.

**Confirmed absent from the graph:** Pillow, pycurl, pycares/aiodns, paramiko/ssh2, libarchive (`pnpm audit`-relevant Next.js too — we're Vite). `nghttpx` and `docker cp` appear nowhere in the repo. The remaining ~35 PoCs are desktop/unrelated-server software (Firefox, ffmpeg, VLC, Ghidra, QEMU, nmap, objdump, 7zip, AnyDesk, RustDesk, Discord, Discourse, Gogs, Gitea, NodeBB, MyBB, NextCloud, PHP, OpenVPN, SystemInformer) — no intersection with DataQ or its CI.

**Two things to carry forward, not act on now:**

1. **Redis 8 is now a gated upgrade.** If we ever bump `redis:7-alpine` → 8, the vector-sets module arrives with it and this becomes live-relevant (no vendor fix exists). Cheap mitigation if we do: don't load the module, keep `--requirepass` + internal ingress.
2. **The Postgres finding is a "don't ever hand out DB roles" constraint.** Our safety here is the single-role model, not a patch. Relevant if multi-tenant DB access is ever considered.

Two honest caveats: these are largely **unpatched** issues, so "not impacted" rests on non-intersection and missing preconditions rather than on us being up to date — there's nothing to bump. And I've taken the repo's technical claims at face value for the impact analysis; I didn't run any PoC. That doesn't change the conclusion, since non-intersection holds whether or not the bugs are real.

No issue filed and no code changed — there's no finding to fix. Say the word if you'd like me to record the Redis-8 gate as a note in `CLAUDE.md` §11 or as a GitHub issue so it isn't rediscovered at upgrade time.

77	### Dependency & CodeQL triage (2026-07-24)
78	
79	A full sweep of the 12 open Dependabot PRs + 6 open CodeQL alerts. **11 of 12 PRs merged**; the twelfth is closed as upstream-blocked.
80	
81	Four of the twelve were not retry-able flakes, and the shape is worth remembering — **a red Dependabot PR is a signal, not noise**:
82	
83	| PR | Looked like | Actually was |
84	|---|---|---|
85	| #958 / #959 (fastapi, fastmcp) | lint failure | Dependabot updates `requirements.txt` **and** `requirements-typecheck.txt`, but never `.pre-commit-config.yaml`'s mypy hook deps — the third place the same pins live. `typecheck-deps-sync` catches it every time. **Structural: any bump of a typecheck-listed package fails this way.** |
86	| #960 (otel exporter) | `ResolutionImpossible` | `opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http==1.44.0` needs `sdk~=1.44`; `azure-monitor-opentelemetry-exporter==1.0.0b55` (**latest**) needs `sdk~=1.43`. No intersection, no version of the Azure exporter accepts 1.44 → **closed, tracked in #970**. The `pip-audit` step burned all 4 retries on it because the loop treats any install failure as a transient PyPI 5xx; a resolution conflict is deterministic. |
87	| #966 (monaco 0.56) | test flake (618 passing) | 0.56 added an `exports` map (`"./*.js": "./esm/vs/*.js"`), making `esm/vs/` implicit — the old deep worker specifier stopped resolving, so the whole test file failed to **load**. Fixed to `monaco-editor/editor/editor.worker.js?worker`; build re-verified to still emit the worker chunk. |
88	
89	**Mid-sweep, three advisories published 2026-07-24 red-lined `pnpm audit` on `main`**, so every open PR failed the gate — including Python-only #963. Fixed in [#971](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/971): js-yaml → 4.3.0, brace-expansion → 1.1.16 / 5.0.8 (**bounded** overrides — an open-ended `>=4.3.0` let pnpm jump js-yaml to the 5.x major), plus a **version-scoped allowlist** for the two with no reachable fix (#968 react-router, #969 brace-expansion 1.x). The allowlist treats a **stale entry as a hard `exit 2`**, so CI demands each waiver's deletion once the dependency moves on — that is what makes #968/#969 self-closing instead of forgotten.
90	
91	Two things only checking could have told me, both recorded because guessing would have gone the other way: forcing brace-expansion 5 everywhere **breaks lint outright** (`minimatch@3` declares `^1.1.7` and calls the default export v5 dropped — `TypeError: expand is not a function`), and monaco's 0.56 worker file **still exists**; only the path to reach it changed. Both new allowlist guards were **mutation-checked** before being trusted.
92	
93	**CodeQL: 6 open → 0.** Only one was a real finding (#56, `py/unnecessary-lambda` in a test — fixed in [#972](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/972)). The other five were dismissed with reasons recorded on each alert: #52/#53/#57/#58 (`py/cyclic-import` in `lineage/`) are the **deliberate** lazy-import registry in `warehouse.py:170-184` — no cycle exists at import time; #61 (`COMPARISON_KIND` unused) is a false positive, the constant is used across 8 modules and the query only sees module-local reads.
94	
95	**Alert cleanup — all three surfaces now at zero** (open PRs 0 · CodeQL 0 · Dependabot 0). The dompurify alert (GHSA-c2j3-45gr-mqc4, low) **auto-closed as `fixed`**: monaco 0.56 (#966) had already pulled dompurify to the patched 3.4.12 transitively. The react-router alert (GHSA-qwww-vcr4-c8h2, high) is dismissed `not_used` with the same unreachability rationale as the audit waiver, tracked in #968.
96	
97	> **Correction — [#974](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/974)'s commit message on `main` is wrong.** It reads *"bump dompurify to 3.4.12 (GHSA-c2j3-45gr-mqc4)"*, but **no bump occurred** — `main` already resolved 3.4.12 via #966, and that PR's lockfile diff is the `overrides:` header line alone, with no resolution change. What it actually did was ratchet the override floor to `>=3.4.12` and add the missing `<4` ceiling (dompurify was the only unbounded entry in the block). The PR body was corrected, but the squash-merge took the single commit's message instead of the PR title, so the bad wording landed and protected-branch history cannot be rewritten — hence this note. Caught by the `/code-review` agent pass. **The tell was there the whole time: a "bump" whose lockfile shows no resolution change bumped nothing** — the audit passing afterwards confirmed the state, not the explanation.
98	
99	Filed from the same session (pre-existing, unrelated to the bumps): [#976](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/976) — the frontend build emits **five** Monaco worker chunks (`ts.worker` alone is 6.9 MB) though `SqlEditorField.tsx` documents that only the base editor worker is needed. Verified identical on 0.55.1, so not a 0.56 regression; `import * as monaco from 'monaco-editor'` pulls every language service. Lazily loaded, so no runtime cost, but ~9 MB of dead artifacts ship each deploy.
100	
101	**The sweep's most useful finding was about the tests, not the dependencies** — [#977](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/977), fixed by [#978](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/978). Verifying the freshly-synced conda env exposed that a bare `pytest -q` with the compose stack down reports `1642 passed, 943 skipped` — while the same commit with Postgres + Redis up reports `2586 passed, 1 skipped`. **About a third of the backend suite was silently not running, and the summary read as success either way.** The skip reasons were always good; pytest just renders them only under `-rs`, and a bare skip count is indistinguishable from the live-datasource tests that legitimately skip without credentials. It also *layers*: bringing up only Postgres moved ~940 tests from skipped to executing, and three then **failed** against a second missing service (Redis backs the SecretStore, so `secret_store.set` raised `SecretWriteError`) — the first layer's skip had concealed the second layer's failure entirely. This directly undercut the verify-locally-before-pushing rule: local green did not mean what CI green meant. #978 keeps the skip behaviour but makes the degradation loud, via a `pytest_terminal_summary` banner (`trylast`) plus a header line.
102	
103	That fix then repeated the session's own lesson twice over. The `/code-review` pass found two defects **my four-state manual walkthrough was structurally incapable of catching**: (1) without `trylast` the banner printed *above* pytest-cov's ~140-line table and scrolled off — invisible to me because every hand-check passed `--no-cov`, so the table that buries it never rendered; (2) `connect_timeout` is libpq-specific, so any non-psycopg URL raised at connect time and got swallowed into a false `NOT REACHABLE` on a perfectly healthy database — invisible because every hand-check used a postgres URL. **Four states looked thorough and shared the same two blind spots**, the same fixture-encodes-the-author's-assumptions shape as #520 and #953. Both are now regression-locked in `backend/tests/test_infra_banner.py` and each was mutation-checked against the un-fixed code rather than trusted green.
104	
105	### Pending design decisions
106	
107	| Decision | Affects | Status |
108	|---|---|---|
109	| Two-connection model for `comparison` checks (**ADR [0015](adr/0015-two-connection-comparison-check-model.md)**, reserved in ADR 0014) | The reconciliation/`comparison` monitor kind — model settled: suite = target under test, check adds one `source_connection_id` ref; build to follow | ✅ decided 2026-07-11 (ADR 0015 written) |
110	
111	### Standing decisions of record & guardrails (carried from the go-live close)
112	
113	| Decision | Record |
114	|---|---|
115	| ADR 0026 (API keys) — **phase 1 (user-scoped PATs) Accepted + built** (v1.1 W1, #461/PR #613; sha256-at-rest rationale in the phase-1 record); service principals stay phase 2; HTTP Basic rejected; the az-CLI pre-auth interim (#565) retires once PATs are the standing headless credential | [ADR 0026](adr/0026-auth-api-keys-and-principal-seam.md) |
116	| Databricks **Free Edition** = demo/eval only; paid workspace before any commercial use | gap **G-h**, [post-v1-roadmap.md](../context/post-v1-roadmap.md) |
117	| **Pre-marketplace harness teardown** — strip Flows A/B/C, the 5 harness connections, demo users, and the seeded-breach check before any marketplace/customer-facing artifact | gap **G-i**, [post-v1-roadmap.md](../context/post-v1-roadmap.md) + `deploy/README.md` |
118	| **Ops/renewal timers consciously skipped** — the Sept-2026 demo-credential cluster self-signals via #419 alerting; recovery = re-mint + KV update | [retro-v1.md](retro-v1.md) |
119	| Key Vault **purge protection left off** (demo-scoped vault) | `deploy/README.md` |
120	| **Recurring cadences stay manual** (weekly security scan — CONTRIBUTING r36, quarterly MCP supply-chain audit — r39 (next ~2026-10-01), Dependabot triage) — no timer infrastructure, run session-driven; extends the ops-timers-skipped decision. Revisit trigger: second contributor or production-critical use. Recorded 2026-07-04 at the `WEEK8_TODO` retirement (its C2 item) | this table (extends [retro-v1.md](retro-v1.md)'s ops-timers decision) |
121	
122	---
123	
124	## Cycle plan — v1.1 (6 weeks + stretch, 2026-07-04 → 2026-08-22)

> **Correction — [#974](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/974)'s commit message on `main` is wrong.** It reads *"bump dompurify to 3.4.12 (GHSA-c2j3-45gr-mqc4)"*, but **no bump occurred** — `main` already resolved 3.4.12 via #966, and that PR's lockfile diff is the `overrides:` header line alone, with no resolution change. What it actually did was ratchet the override floor to `>=3.4.12` and add the missing `<4` ceiling (dompurify was the only unbounded entry in the block). The PR body was corrected, but the squash-merge took the single commit's message instead of the PR title, so the bad wording landed and protected-branch history cannot be rewritten — hence this note. Caught by the `/code-review` agent pass. **The tell was there the whole time: a "bump" whose lockfile shows no resolution change bumped nothing** — the audit passing afterwards confirmed the state, not the explanation.

Filed from the same session (pre-existing, unrelated to the bumps): [#976](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/976) — the frontend build emits **five** Monaco worker chunks (`ts.worker` alone is 6.9 MB) though `SqlEditorField.tsx` documents that only the base editor worker is needed. Verified identical on 0.55.1, so not a 0.56 regression; `import * as monaco from 'monaco-editor'` pulls every language service. Lazily loaded, so no runtime cost, but ~9 MB of dead artifacts ship each deploy.

**The sweep's most useful finding was about the tests, not the dependencies** — [#977](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/977), fixed by [#978](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/978). Verifying the freshly-synced conda env exposed that a bare `pytest -q` with the compose stack down reports `1642 passed, 943 skipped` — while the same commit with Postgres + Redis up reports `2586 passed, 1 skipped`. **About a third of the backend suite was silently not running, and the summary read as success either way.** The skip reasons were always good; pytest just renders them only under `-rs`, and a bare skip count is indistinguishable from the live-datasource tests that legitimately skip without credentials. It also *layers*: bringing up only Postgres moved ~940 tests from skipped to executing, and three then **failed** against a second missing service (Redis backs the SecretStore, so `secret_store.set` raised `SecretWriteError`) — the first layer's skip had concealed the second layer's failure entirely. This directly undercut the verify-locally-before-pushing rule: local green did not mean what CI green meant. #978 keeps the skip behaviour but makes the degradation loud, via a `pytest_terminal_summary` banner (`trylast`) plus a header line.

That fix then repeated the session's own lesson twice over. The `/code-review` pass found two defects **my four-state manual walkthrough was structurally incapable of catching**: (1) without `trylast` the banner printed *above* pytest-cov's ~140-line table and scrolled off — invisible to me because every hand-check passed `--no-cov`, so the table that buries it never rendered; (2) `connect_timeout` is libpq-specific, so any non-psycopg URL raised at connect time and got swallowed into a false `NOT REACHABLE` on a perfectly healthy database — invisible because every hand-check used a postgres URL. **Four states looked thorough and shared the same two blind spots**, the same fixture-encodes-the-author's-assumptions shape as #520 and #953. Both are now regression-locked in `backend/tests/test_infra_banner.py` and each was mutation-checked against the un-fixed code rather than trusted green.

### Pending design decisions

| Decision | Affects | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Two-connection model for `comparison` checks (**ADR [0015](adr/0015-two-connection-comparison-check-model.md)**, reserved in ADR 0014) | The reconciliation/`comparison` monitor kind — model settled: suite = target under test, check adds one `source_connection_id` ref; build to follow | ✅ decided 2026-07-11 (ADR 0015 written) |

| **Ops/renewal timers consciously skipped** — the Sept-2026 demo-credential cluster self-signals via #419 alerting; recovery = re-mint + KV update | [retro-v1.md](retro-v1.md) |

| **Recurring cadences stay manual** (weekly security scan — CONTRIBUTING r36, quarterly MCP supply-chain audit — r39 (next ~2026-10-01), Dependabot triage) — no timer infrastructure, run session-driven; extends the ops-timers-skipped decision. Revisit trigger: second contributor or production-critical use. Recorded 2026-07-04 at the `WEEK8_TODO` retirement (its C2 item) | this table (extends [retro-v1.md](retro-v1.md)'s ops-timers decision) |

# Security & data handling

How DataQ authenticates users, stores secrets, handles the data it sees, and what it keeps.
This is a plain-language overview for people evaluating or operating DataQ. It is **not** a
legal compliance certification — much of GDPR/HIPAA is organizational (DPAs, BAAs, consent,
lawful basis) and is the deploying organization's responsibility.

## Authentication & access

- **Single sign-on (OIDC).** Users sign in through your identity provider; DataQ is
  provider-neutral (validated against Azure AD). The backend validates the token on every
  request — there is no local password store.
- **Personal access tokens (PATs).** For headless / AI-client use, users mint `dq_live_`
  tokens ([API keys](api-keys.md)). Tokens are **hashed (SHA-256) at rest** — the plaintext is
  shown once and never stored — and carry the **same authz as the user**, on REST and MCP.
  They can be scoped with an expiry and revoked.
- **Per-suite authorization.** Access is granted per suite (**view / edit**); a caller only
  ever sees suites they own or are shared on. There are no ambient "see everything" reads
  except the workspace-admin role below.
- **Workspace admins.** An allowlisted role (`WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`) with workspace-wide
  visibility over every suite, its results, and schedules (ADR 0027). Because that includes
  failing-row samples (the one place PII can appear), **keep the allowlist minimal** and treat
  a data-access audit trail as a prerequisite before granting it in a regulated deployment.

## Network exposure

- The **frontend is the only public surface**; the API runs on **internal ingress** and is
  reached only through the frontend's same-origin `/api`, `/healthz`, and `/mcp` proxy
  (ADR 0028 §5). All traffic is over **HTTPS/TLS**.
- The **MCP** AI-assistant endpoint is **fail-closed** — unauthenticated requests are rejected
  (ADR 0008).

## Secrets

- Datasource credentials, webhook signing keys, and channel secrets are held in a **secret
  store behind a seam** — Azure Key Vault in the reference deployment — never in the database
  or in git. The app reads them via a managed identity.
- Secret **references** (names), not secret values, are stored alongside connections. Deleting
  a connection removes its secret (soft-delete on Key Vault).
- Inbound webhooks are authenticated: ADF by a shared secret, Airflow and dbt by an
  **HMAC-SHA256** signature keyed on a stored signing key.

## The data DataQ sees, stores, and redacts

DataQ runs checks *against* your data; it is **not** a copy of your data. What it persists:

- **Metadata** — suites, checks, connection config (no secrets), schedules, trigger bindings.
- **Results** — per-check pass/fail + a numeric `metric_value`, and for failing checks a
  small **failing-row sample**.
- **Failing-row samples are the one place results can carry PII/PHI.** They are **redacted at
  the boundary, column-aware**: a suite's **column policy** (auto-derived by a classifier or
  set by hand) keeps non-sensitive breach values debuggable while masking PII columns to
  `<redacted>`. The numeric counts and row/column shape are kept.
- **Logs & traces** are PII-redacted at the logger level, and secret values never enter them.

## Retention

- Failing-row **samples are purged** after a retention window (PII-minimisation), while the
  aggregatable **`metric_value` history is kept** for trends and baselines — so you lose the
  raw rows but keep the signal.

## Encryption

- **In transit:** HTTPS/TLS everywhere (public ingress and the internal proxy hop).
- **At rest:** provided by the managed data services — PostgreSQL, the object stores, and Key
  Vault all encrypt at rest in the reference (Azure) deployment.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please report suspected security issues privately to the maintainers rather than opening a
public issue.

---

*For the detailed technical-controls-vs-regulation gap analysis (an internal engineering
document, not a certification), maintainers keep a separate compliance-posture register.*

=== postgres.tf role/priv context ===
# App database — a DISTINCT `dataq` database on the SHARED Postgres Flexible Server
# (this subscription caps Flexible Servers at 1, so the app shares the harness's
# server — renamed neutrally to dataq-pg-* / purpose=dataq-shared). The app connects
# as the least-privilege `dataq_app` role, which OWNS only the `dataq` database (no
# access to the `airflow` metadata DB on the same server).
#
# The `dataq_app` role + `dataq` database are provisioned out-of-band (a one-off
# psql against the server — see deploy/terraform/README.md "Shared Postgres"),
# keeping this stack connection-free (no postgres provider / no plan-time DB
# connection, so it stays CI-friendly). Its password is passed in as the sensitive
# var.app_db_password and injected as the DATABASE_URL Container App secret.
#
# Runtime reachability: the ACA apps connect over the server's allow-Azure-services
# firewall rule (the apps are Azure services), same as airflow.

data "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server" "shared" {
  name                = var.shared_pg_server_name
  resource_group_name = data.azurerm_resource_group.dataq.name
}

locals {
  # psycopg2 URL the backend Settings read as DATABASE_URL. sslmode=require —
  # Flexible Server enforces TLS. The password is URL-encoded so a future value
  # containing URL-significant chars (@ : / ? #) can't break DSN parsing (#395);
  # app_db_user/name are controlled alnum identifiers, no encoding needed.
  database_url = join("", [
    "postgresql+psycopg2://",
    var.app_db_user, ":", urlencode(var.app_db_password),
    "@", data.azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server.shared.fqdn, ":5432/",
    var.app_db_name, "?sslmode=require",
  ])
}

input.command:
gh issue create --repo TheurgicDuke771/DataQ \
  --title "Redis 8 upgrade gate: keep the Vector Sets module unloaded (unpatched RCE class)" \
  --label security --label ops --label "priority/P3" \
  --milestone "v1.1 Backlog" \
  --body 'Not a live vulnerability — a **precondition to check before a future bump**. Filed so it is not rediscovered at upgrade time.

## Context

Triaged 2026-07-24 against [`bikini/exploitarium`](https://github.com/bikini/exploitarium), a public archive of ~44 largely-unreported PoCs. DataQ is **not impacted today**, but one entry becomes live-relevant the moment we move Redis off 7.x.

`redis-vset-duplicate-hnsw-id-rce-poc` is a full RCE: duplicate HNSW node IDs in a `RESTORE`d Vector Set alias distinct node objects, `VREM` leaves a stale link, `VLINKS ... WITHSCORES` becomes a 64-bit read oracle, and `hnsw_reconnect_nodes()` overwrites a module value whose `free` pointer is then dispatched by `freeModuleObject()`. **No vendor fix exists.**

## Why we are safe now

The Vector Sets module ships bundled from **Redis 8**. We run `redis:7-alpine` in both places, so the `VSET`/`VLINKS` command surface does not exist:

- [`deploy/terraform/azure/redis.tf:43`](deploy/terraform/azure/redis.tf#L43)
- [`docker-compose.yml:33`](docker-compose.yml#L33)

Defence in depth already present: `external_enabled = false` (internal ingress only) plus `--requirepass`. The PoC needs an authenticated client, so both would have to fail together.

## The gate

Dependabot does **not** watch Docker images (`.github/dependabot.yml` has pip/npm/github-actions only), so a Redis server bump is always a deliberate human edit — which is exactly why this needs a tracked reminder rather than automation.

Before merging any bump of the Redis **server** image to 8.x:

- [ ] Confirm the vector-sets module is not loaded (Redis 8 bundles it; verify with `MODULE LIST` on the running container, do not assume the default)
- [ ] If it is present, either disable module loading or check whether the duplicate-HNSW-ID path has been fixed upstream by then
- [ ] Keep `--requirepass` and `external_enabled = false` regardless
- [ ] Re-read this issue rather than trusting that "the image built and Celery connected" — a green broker proves reachability, not that the command surface is absent

Note the distinct, unrelated pin already in `dependabot.yml`: **redis-py** 8.x majors are ignored because `kombu[redis]` caps `redis<6.5`. That is the *client* library. This issue is about the *server* image; do not let one be read as covering the other.

# Runtime reachability: the ACA apps connect over the server's allow-Azure-services
# firewall rule (the apps are Azure services), same as airflow.
#
# SECURITY CONSTRAINT — the single-role model is load-bearing, not just tidy.
# PostgreSQL's referential-integrity check switches to the REFERENCED TABLE'S OWNER
# before invoking an implicit cast on the FK value (ri_triggers.c). A role that can
# CREATE TYPE / FUNCTION / CAST and holds REFERENCES on another owner's table can
# therefore run its own SQL as that owner — reaching COPY ... TO PROGRAM if the owner
# has pg_execute_server_program. Unpatched upstream as of 2026-07-24.
# We are not exposed because there is exactly ONE app role (`dataq_app`) and it is
# not shared with any untrusted party. Adding a second, less-trusted role to the
# `dataq` database is what would create the exposure — so do not, without revisiting
# this. See the guardrail row in docs/progress.md.

# App database — a DISTINCT `dataq` database on the SHARED Postgres Flexible Server
# (this subscription caps Flexible Servers at 1, so the app shares the harness's
# server — renamed neutrally to dataq-pg-* / purpose=dataq-shared). The app connects
# as the least-privilege `dataq_app` role, which OWNS only the `dataq` database (no
# access to the `airflow` metadata DB on the same server).
#
# The `dataq_app` role + `dataq` database are provisioned out-of-band (a one-off
# psql against the server — see deploy/terraform/README.md "Shared Postgres"),
# keeping this stack connection-free (no postgres provider / no plan-time DB
# connection, so it stays CI-friendly). Its password is passed in as the sensitive
# var.app_db_password and injected as the DATABASE_URL Container App secret.
#
# Runtime reachability: the ACA apps connect over the server's allow-Azure-services
# firewall rule (the apps are Azure services), same as airflow.

data "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server" "shared" {
  name                = var.shared_pg_server_name
  resource_group_name = data.azurerm_resource_group.dataq.name
}

locals {
  # psycopg2 URL the backend Settings read as DATABASE_URL. sslmode=require —
  # Flexible Server enforces TLS. The password is URL-encoded so a future value
  # containing URL-significant chars (@ : / ? #) can't break DSN parsing (#395);
  # app_db_user/name are controlled alnum identifiers, no encoding needed.
  database_url = join("", [
    "postgresql+psycopg2://",
    var.app_db_user, ":", urlencode(var.app_db_password),
    "@", data.azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server.shared.fqdn, ":5432/",
    var.app_db_name, "?sslmode=require",
  ])
}

input.new_string:
### Upstream 0-day triage — `bikini/exploitarium` (2026-07-24)

Triaged the public [`bikini/exploitarium`](https://github.com/bikini/exploitarium) archive (~44 PoCs, 12 assigned CVEs in its `cves.md`, the rest claimed unreported) against DataQ's actual dependency graph. **Verdict: not impacted — no code change warranted.** Recorded because *why* we are safe is not obvious from the code, and two of the reasons are conditions that could quietly stop holding.

The four entries that touch our stack and why each misses:

| PoC | Our reality | Why it misses |
|---|---|---|
| `redis-vset-duplicate-hnsw-id-rce` (RCE) | `redis:7-alpine` | The Vector Sets module ships from Redis **8**; 7.x has no `VSET`/`VLINKS` surface. Also needs an authenticated client — broker is internal-ingress + `--requirepass`. **→ [#980](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/980)** |
| `postgres-ri-owner-switched-cast` (RCE) | one least-priv `dataq_app` role | Needs a hostile DB role with `CREATE TYPE/FUNCTION/CAST` + `REFERENCES`, *and* a referenced-table owner in `pg_execute_server_program`. Neither exists; Azure Flexible Server does not grant the latter. |
| `curl-smtp-expn-recipient-crlf-injection` | `smtplib`, not libcurl (`alerting/email.py`) | Different code path — and our own analogous exposure is already closed: user-supplied recipients are CR/LF-rejected at write time by `_UNSAFE_IN_RECIPIENT` (`notification_service.py`, from the #639 review). |
| `flowise-mcp-env-case-bypass` | FastMCP **server** at `/mcp` | Flowise spawns stdio children from user config past a case-sensitive env denylist; we never spawn a child process from user input. |

That last one is a *class* rather than a package match — a case-sensitive allow/denylist matched against a case-insensitive value — so the three equivalents in our code were checked rather than assumed: webhook SSRF hosts lowercase both the config side (`notification_service.py:58`) and the parsed URL host (`:83`), and the workspace-admin allowlist matches case-insensitively (`auth.py:283`). All three are allowlists, so the failure mode is fail-closed either way.

Confirmed absent from the graph rather than eyeballed: Pillow, pycurl, pycares/aiodns, paramiko/ssh2, libarchive, Next.js (we are Vite). `nghttpx` and `docker cp` appear nowhere in the repo. The remaining ~35 PoCs are desktop or unrelated-server software with no intersection.

**Two caveats kept deliberately.** These are largely **unpatched**, so "not impacted" rests on non-intersection and missing preconditions — there is nothing to bump, and no green audit will ever confirm this the way `pip-audit` confirms a CVE. And the repo's technical claims were taken at face value; no PoC was run. Neither changes the verdict, since non-intersection holds whether or not the bugs are real.

### Pending design decisions
